analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and raises federal Medicaid matching funds for those services.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since it was referred there on June 12, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today excludes routine dental, vision, and hearing care, leaving beneficiaries to pay out of pocket or buy separate private coverage. This bill would cover cleanings, fillings, root canals, dentures, eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, hearing exams, and hearing aids under Medicare, with yearly limits on some services. It would also raise the federal Medicaid matching rate to 90% for states covering those services for adults. The federal payment share starts low and phases up to 80% only in the eighth year after enactment, and the bill includes no provision to pay for the added federal spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare enrollees, who currently pay 100% of dental, vision, and hearing costs out of pocket or buy separate private coverage, would get federally covered care with capped frequency limits and a gradually rising federal payment share. State Medicaid programs that cover adult dental, vision, and hearing services would get a 90% federal match for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare enrollees and adult Medicaid beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds routine cleanings and exams, basic services like fillings and crowns, major services like root canals and extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures to Medicare's covered services [S2] [S3].
It adds routine eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, low-vision devices, routine hearing exams, and hearing aids to Medicare coverage, replacing the current statutory exclusions [S2] [S3].
It raises the federal Medicaid match to 90% for dental, vision, and hearing services furnished to adults, reducing the state share for programs that cover them [S2] [S3].

The bill caps out-of-pocket exposure with frequency limits: two cleanings and two dental exams per year, dentures once every five years, one eye exam and one pair of lenses per year, one frame every two years, a $200 contact-lens allowance per two years, and one hearing aid per ear every four years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the added cost of the new Medicare benefit and the richer Medicaid match; the bill text contains no offsetting revenue or savings. Medicare enrollees would still owe the unpaid share of costs during a phase-in in which the federal payment percentage starts at 0% the first year and reaches 80% only in the eighth year after enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and, during the ramp-up, beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: The bill text contains no financing: it adds a large new federal entitlement with no taxes, premiums, or spending cuts to offset it, so the cost lands on the deficit and taxpayers [S3].

The phase-in is slow: Medicare pays 0% of allowed charges in the first year and does not reach 80% until the eighth year after enactment, leaving beneficiaries bearing most of the cost for years [S3].

Coverage is limited: the Secretary of Health and Human Services may impose prior authorization and further limits on every category of care, and may scale coverage back to recommendations of the US Preventive Services Task Force [S3].

The Medicaid improvement is a matching-rate increase, not a mandate: states only benefit if they choose to cover adult dental, vision, and hearing services, and states that do not cover them see no change for their residents [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For older and disabled Americans, filling one of Medicare's largest coverage gaps is a substantial benefit — untreated dental disease, uncorrected vision, and unaddressed hearing loss are common and costly in this population. But the design is hard to defend as written: a benefit that pays nothing in year one and only 80% after seven years delays most of the help indefinitely, and with no financing attached the bill would add significant federal spending with no plan for how to pay for it. An honest supporter would want a faster phase-in and an identified funding source.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 12, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it; Congress is still in session, so it remains sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks introduced the bill in the Senate on June 12, 2025, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Fetterman, Merkley, and Welch [S3] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since [S1] [S5].

The bill would amend Medicare's covered-services and exclusion provisions so that dental, vision, and hearing care — currently excluded by statute — becomes covered, with special payment rules and frequency limits [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled, the coverage status quo is preserved: Medicare Advantage plans keep using dental, vision, and hearing extras as a selling point for their private plans, and standalone dental and vision insurance keeps its market. Medicare enrollees continue to pay the full cost of dental, vision, and hearing care themselves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers selling dental, vision, and hearing add-on coverage

for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 2084 on June 12, 2025 and shepherded its referral to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, the bill's entire Senate support as shown on the record.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 12, 2025 and has taken no further action on it since; no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever occurred, so there is no recorded opposition; all five original sponsors are Democrats and the bill sits in the Republican-chaired Finance Committee without a hearing [S3] [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Dentists, dental labs, and dental practices
industries.note: A new Medicare dental benefit would make tens of millions of enrollees insured dental patients, with Medicare paying up to 80% of allowed charges after the phase-in. Seniors gain coverage and providers gain paying customers at the same time.

Medicare coverage of hearing exams and hearing aids (one per ear every four years) would create a large new federally funded customer base. The industry benefits directly alongside the beneficiaries the bill is meant to help.
Coverage of annual eye exams, one pair of lenses a year, and a $200 two-year contact-lens allowance would route routine vision care through Medicare payment. Providers gain a newly insured market.

industries.industry: Standalone dental, vision, and hearing insurance
industries.note: Private plans selling dental, vision, and hearing coverage to seniors, plus discount plans, exist because Medicare excludes these services. Universal Medicare coverage would erode or eliminate much of that market — which is exactly the point of the bill.

MA plans currently attract enrollees by offering dental, vision, and hearing extras that original Medicare lacks. Adding those benefits to original Medicare shrinks that selling point, though the plans would be required to fold in the new benefit as well.

analysis.trajectory: Bills adding dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare have been introduced repeatedly across Congresses and none has cleared the Finance Committee, which must move any Medicare benefit change. With no Republican cosponsors, no hearing scheduled months after referral, and no financing attached, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress.
